Antes de convertirme, nunca había oído el término «anabaptista», y me era ajena la idea de que alguien compartiera su fe en Jesús con otras personas. Después de convertirme, recuerdo que pensaba en todos mis amigos que no sabían nada de lo que acababa de sucederme. Una cosa no dejaba de darme vueltas en la cabeza: «¡Tengo que contárselo!». Cuando a alguien le sucede algo bueno, normalmente se lo cuenta a los demás. Algunos se lo cuentan a una o dos personas, mientras que otros sienten deseos de contárselo a todo el mundo. Eso era lo que yo quería hacer, no por mí, sino por ellos.

Cada vez que veía a un viejo amigo, le contaba lo que me había sucedido. Por lo general, me decían que ya lo habían oído y luego intentaban hacer que me calmara y me relajara. Seré el primero en admitir que cometí errores durante esos primeros años. Noté que a muchas personas no les agradaba lo que yo tenía que decir, pero lo que más me asombró fue que quienes afirmaban ser cristianos parecían ser los más ofendidos.

Un día estaba conversando con un hombre mayor que dijo que había sido cristiano durante casi toda su vida. Durante la conversación, señaló una bombilla y dijo: «¿Ve esa bombilla? No habla». Me quedé atónito. Me estaba diciendo que sí, Jesús dice que somos la luz del mundo, pero que las luces guardan silencio. No hablan. Me fui a casa para estudiar el tema en la Biblia por mi cuenta. ¿Era cierto? No tardé en encontrar versículos como este: Y recorrió Jesús toda Galilea, enseñando en las sinagogas de ellos, predicando el evangelio del reino y sanando toda enfermedad y toda dolencia entre el pueblo. –Mat 4:23. Además, en Mateo, Jesús dice que se compadeció porque la gente que estaba con él estaba cansada y dispersa. Más adelante leemos: Entonces dijo a sus discípulos: La mies es mucha, pero los obreros pocos. Rogad, pues, al Señor de la mies que envíe obreros a su mies. –Mat 9:37-38

Me parece que, adondequiera que iba Jesús, hablaba con la gente acerca del reino. He visto a personas dar testimonio de Dios, pero hacerlo de una manera desagradable. Eso no significa que no debamos dar testimonio. Si leen el libro de los Hechos, eso es prácticamente todo lo que ven: ¡creyentes compartiendo el mensaje del Evangelio con los demás! En un relato, las autoridades arrestaron a los discípulos y les dijeron que podían quedar libres si se callaban. Pero los discípulos dijeron que no podían: porque no podemos dejar de decir lo que hemos visto y oído. –Act 4:20. Con el tiempo, los silenciaron para siempre: con la muerte.

Más tarde oí hablar de estas personas llamadas anabaptistas. Empecé a leer sobre ellos y sobre cómo tampoco ellos se callaban. Pedí el Martyr’s Mirror y me asombró lo que leí. Estas queridas personas vivieron como los discípulos que encontramos en la Biblia. Cumplieron lo que Jesús dijo: Y seréis aborrecidos de todos por causa de mi nombre; mas el que persevere hasta el fin, este será salvo. –Mat 10:22. Y en Romanos: Como está escrito: Por causa de ti somos muertos todo el tiempo; somos contados como ovejas para el matadero. –Rom 8:36. Al cabo de un tiempo, encontré una iglesia con una visión anabaptista.

Entonces, ¿por qué escribo esto? Queridos hermanos y hermanas, creo que el fuego se está apagando. Sigo oyendo a algunos de nuestros anabaptistas hablar de llevar una vida tranquila y apacible. Jesús nos dice en la parábola del sembrador: Asimismo, el que fue sembrado entre espinos, este es el que oye la palabra, pero el afán de este mundo y el engaño de las riquezas ahogan la palabra, y queda sin fruto. –Mat 13:22. ¿Será que algunos de nosotros estamos en esa situación? Vivimos en una cultura occidental en la que parece fácil conseguir dinero, y nos enfocamos en nuestras propias riquezas y en los afanes de este mundo. Tengamos cuidado de no volvernos como el mundo para evitar que el mundo nos persiga.

Un grupo de anabaptistas huía de la persecución y se trasladó a un país donde todavía no se les perseguía. Abrieron una tienda de muebles para mantenerse, pero no podían vender ningún mueble porque eran los temidos anabaptistas. Pronto la situación se volvió desesperada porque necesitaban dinero para comprar comida. Un día, un hombre rico entró en la tienda. Todos los trabajadores dejaron de trabajar. «¡Quizás este hombre compre algo y podamos comer!», pensaron. Un hermano anciano se acercó al posible cliente y le preguntó si conocía a Jesús. Después de una breve conversación, el hombre salió de la tienda furioso. Al poco tiempo, unos trabajadores hambrientos le preguntaron al anciano por qué había tenido que ahuyentar su única oportunidad de vender algo. Él explicó que era mucho más importante que ese hombre conociera a Jesús que preocuparse por hacer una venta. Esa era la mentalidad de los primeros anabaptistas: el Evangelio era lo primero. No podían dejar de hablar de las cosas que habían visto y oído, y a ellos también los mataban todo el tiempo.

He leído numerosos relatos de los primeros cristianos anabaptistas que fueron arrestados por su fe. Las autoridades les suplicaban que simplemente se callaran. Pero ellos se negaban, tal como hicieron los discípulos. También eligieron la muerte antes que una vida tranquila. Arrestaron a un joven que dejó atrás a su querida esposa, embarazada de su primer hijo. Las autoridades esperaron a que naciera el niño y luego llevaron al recién nacido a su padre, que estaba en prisión. Le dijeron que ahora era padre y que podía irse a casa para estar con su esposa y su hijo. También le dijeron que podía seguir creyendo lo mismo, pero que debía guardar silencio y no hablar contra el pecado en la iglesia. El joven padre se negó, así que lo quemaron en la hoguera. Guardar silencio no era una opción.

Entonces, ¿qué quieren decir las Escrituras con una vida tranquila y apacible? Pablo escribe a Timoteo: Exhorto, pues, ante todo, a que se hagan súplicas, oraciones, intercesiones y acciones de gracias por todos los hombres, por los reyes y por todos los que están en autoridad; para que llevemos una vida tranquila y apacible, con toda piedad y dignidad. –1Ti 2:1-2. ¿Por los reyes y por todos los que están en autoridad, para que llevemos una vida tranquila y apacible, con toda piedad y dignidad? Sí, el apóstol Pablo dice esto, pero ¿qué quiso decir? ¿Quiso decir que debemos callarnos acerca del Evangelio? ¿O que nunca debemos confrontar a un pecador? Pablo no nos dice que hagamos algo que él nunca hizo ni algo que Cristo mismo nunca hizo. De hecho, las Escrituras revelan algo muy distinto.

Parece que los cristianos del Nuevo Testamento que aparecen en la Biblia y en la iglesia primitiva difundían activamente el Evangelio y estaban entusiasmados con la Iglesia de Jesucristo. Iban predicando el Evangelio: celebraban reuniones en las montañas, en los bosques o dondequiera que acudiera la gente. Esa era su vida. Aquí Pablo está diciendo que debemos orar para que, si obedecemos a Dios haciendo cosas que no les gustan a las autoridades, estas nos dejen tranquilos mientras realizamos nuestras actividades cotidianas. Como cristianos, debemos difundir la verdad de la Palabra de Dios y trabajar activamente para el avance del Reino de Dios. Debemos orar para que las autoridades nos permitan vivir en paz mientras servimos al Príncipe de Paz.

Algunos cristianos intentan ser como el mundo en sus esfuerzos por ganar al mundo: intentan lograr que la gente viva feliz, se una a nuestro grupo, sea libre en Cristo, participe en un emocionante viaje misionero, disfrute de la vida al máximo y llegue a ser todo lo que pueda. Todo gira en torno a «amar a Jesús», no a obedecerlo.

¿Y nosotros? ¿Nos entusiasma hablarle a la gente de Jesús, incluso si eso nos cuesta algo? Para muchos de nosotros es muy fácil hablar de agricultura, construcción, caza de ciervos y muchas otras cosas; sin embargo, cuando se trata de las cosas de Dios, tenemos poco que decir. ¿Tenemos tanto miedo de la persecución? ¿Tememos que el mundo nos odie? Recuerden lo que dijo Jesús: Si el mundo os aborrece, sabed que a mí me ha aborrecido antes que a vosotros. Si fuerais del mundo, el mundo amaría lo suyo… –Joh 15:18-19. Y también: Porque el que se avergonzare de mí y de mis palabras en esta generación adúltera y pecadora, también el Hijo del Hombre se avergonzará de él cuando venga en la gloria de su Padre con los santos ángeles. –Mar 8:38

Es fácil ser cristiano si uno se instala y lleva una vida tranquila y apacible, sin desafiar nunca a un pecador, sin corregir nunca a un hermano y sin pisarle nunca los callos a Satanás; pero ¿quién dijo que sería fácil? Aquí en Haití, como iglesia, intentamos seguir a Jesús sin importar el costo. Apenas ayer, dos miembros nos dijeron que están a punto de perder sus empleos por causa del Evangelio. Otra hermana de la iglesia informó que la escuela a la que asisten sus hijos exige uniformes y que las niñas deben llevar pantalones. Envió a su hija a la escuela con un vestido modesto, pero la enviaron de regreso a casa con una nota del director que decía que no debía volver a la escuela con «esa cosa». Si sois vituperados por el nombre de Cristo, sois bienaventurados, porque el Espíritu de gloria y de Dios reposa sobre vosotros. Por parte de ellos, él es blasfemado, pero por parte de vosotros, es glorificado. –1Pe 4:14

La felicidad proviene de sufrir por causa de la justicia. El sufrimiento bíblico proviene de obedecer a Jesús frente a la oposición. ¿Estamos demasiado ocupados discutiendo por opiniones doctrinales personales y tratando de ser políticamente correctos mientras el mundo se ríe de nosotros y se va al infierno? Seamos como Jesús y como los cristianos fieles de todas las épocas, y vivamos de tal manera que quienes nos rodean no puedan negar que el poder de Dios está en nosotros. Tenemos algo que todos necesitan. Entonces, ¿qué esperamos? ¡Reunámonos de nuevo, volvamos a juntarnos, neguémonos a nosotros mismos, tomemos nuestras cruces y sigámoslo!

As we have been developing this article over the last year, we have become increasingly aware of a growing interest in this subject. Various papers and booklets have been, or are being, written about it. Some writings debate specific theories of the atonement, while others reason about various terms or Bible verses. What ideas and statements concerning the atonement are found in the clear teachings of Scripture, and which are misunderstandings or wrong interpretations?

I. The Atonement

The term atonement is usually understood to explain all or part of what happened spiritually (for the believer) when Christ went through His suffering, death, and resurrection. Sometimes the term atonement is used to define that which brings men and women to a place of “at-one-ment” (to be at one) with God. How does that event in history still affect us today, some 2,000 years later?

In these discussions, there is the tendency to forget that the finished work of Christ includes multiple aspects, with each one contributing to a different effect for the believer today. These different aspects include Christ’s Suffering, His Blood, His Death, His Burial, His Resurrection, and His Ascension.

a. His Suffering

His suffering covers the physical, emotional, and mental anguish He endured that culminated with His death on the cross. Here we see that …it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day … that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name… –Luk 24:46-47. The suffering servant, as portrayed in the whole of Isaiah chapter 53, gives a vivid picture of this aspect of the atonement. Isaiah describes Him as being …wounded for our transgressions, [and] …bruised for our iniquities: –Isa 53:5. Here we also have the reality that with his stripes we are healed. –Isa 53:5. Finally, we see that He was oppressed, and he was afflicted… –Isa 53:7, and that he endured … travail of his soul… –Isa 53:11

Let’s note a few more of the many passages that speak of His suffering: For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God… –1Pe 3:18; Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered –Heb 5:8; For it became him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things, in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings –Heb 2:10.

A sometimes forgotten purpose of Jesus’ suffering is that, as believers, we are to identify with His suffering as given in the following passages: For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ –2Co 1:5; …if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together –Rom 8:17; That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death –Php 3:10.

b. His Blood that was Shed

The blood of Christ being shed for the atonement of sinful man needs some careful consideration as a specific vital aspect of the whole. Of course, it is included in points a. and c., but the Scriptures also give much attention to this particular part. It would perhaps require a whole book to expound on this aspect, but we should note one thing on this point. It is with the shedding of the blood of Jesus that we have God’s specific solution for the remission of our sins given here in Jesus’ own words, For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins –Mat 26:28.

In Hebrews chapters 9 and 10, we have very detailed explanation showing how the “blood sacrifices” of the Old Testament were not perfect in themselves, rather they were a “type” that pointed forward to the perfect sacrifice—Jesus, the Lamb of God. It is in this context that we have this—that …almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission. –Heb 9:22. This is particularly important to remember when we consider that some people claim that God could just simply forgive sin without death or the shedding of blood if He so chose. These people use the story found in Matthew 18:23-35 as their proof text. It would do us well to consider that this story is revealing the “why” (compassion) of the outcome, not the “how” of the details. We cannot take this story out of context of Scripture and build a doctrine that undermines all the rest of Scripture. Thus, we conclude that in God’s economy He has ordained that sin must be washed away with the blood of Christ—And from Jesus Christ, who … washed us from our sins in his own blood, –Rev 1:5.

For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God –Rom 3:23-25. Here we see that for anyone of us that has sinned (ALL of us), we have our propitiation made possible through faith in His (Jesus’) blood.

c. His Death

Jesus said, …I lay down my life for the sheep –Joh 10:15, and again He said, …I lay down my life, that I might take it again. No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again… –Joh 10:17-18.

But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour; that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man. For it became him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things, in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings. –Heb 2:9-10. When you partake of communion …ye do shew the Lord’s death till he come –1Co 11:26.

Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. –Rom 6:3-4

It is during this period of Jesus’ time on earth that the earthly, mortal part of Him separated from that which was heavenly, eternal, and immortal.

d. His Burial

We note again, as referenced above, the truth that Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death… –Rom. 6:4. While all these aspects are a part of the whole, the burial represents …a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die… –Joh 12:24. First is the ending of life (pouring out of the blood), then death, then burial, then resurrection. The burial part is the confirmation that death has occurred. It brings finality, closure, and an end to the former. It is the necessary interval between death and resurrection.

It is also the time of Jesus’ entrance into Hades, the place of departed souls, of which we are given only glimpses through several passages of Scripture.

e. His Resurrection

In His resurrection we are raised with Him in newness of life. (Romans 6:4) …wherein also ye are risen with him through the faith of the operation of God, who hath raised him from the dead –Col 2:12. So, in His resurrection we are raised up with Him from death (if we were dead prior) and are provided the power to walk in newness of life (the power to have victory over sin).

f. His Ascension

In His ascension we understand that …he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight. –Act 1:9. It is due to His leaving this earth that we have many key aspects for the believer’s life today. There is the provision of the Holy Spirit made possible once Jesus left this earth. We have the promise of His going to prepare a better home for us to someday join Him in everlasting joy. We have Jesus sitting at the right hand of the throne of God interceding for us. We have Jesus acting in the role of our sympathetic High Priest, one that knows and understands our every need and struggle, since He has the experience of living on the sinful earth inside a mortal body.

Herein, we start to see how each part of the Atonement achieves a different result for the believer and that each part is only that—A PART. A part of the whole. A part of the finished work of Christ. These lists could each go on and fill page after page of all the blessings and benefits each one enables for the believer. For the sake of space, we will stop on this part for now and continue with the rest of the article, but hopefully this will stimulate each of us to further meditation in God’s Word on these matters.

II. Common statements that are not Biblically correct

There are some popular statements which we may hear concerning the atonement that do not accurately describe what the Scriptures teach. But because they are popular in our conversations, or perhaps they’re even the words of a familiar song, they may skew our understanding of the finished work of Christ. For some examples, let’s look at the following statements:

a. “Christ took my place on Calvary.”

This may seem like a logical conclusion, because He died for us, …the just for the unjust… –1Pe 3:18. and He died that we might live. There is no question that it was for us, but the preposition, for, can be understood several different ways. It can mean in my place, or it can mean on my behalf. Most of Scripture clearly emphasizes that He died on my behalf, but less clear is the idea of a direct substitution. Emphasizing substitution leads us to the following concept: He died in my place, so I don’t need to. If this becomes the primary way of thinking about the atonement, we may miss what is equally important—that since He died, so I must also die with Him. See Rom 6:1-11

b. “The guilt of my sin was placed on Christ.”

There are passages that speak of Christ bearing our sins. So Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many… –Heb 9:28 and, Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree… –1Pe 2:24. But what is the proper understanding of what it means to ‘bear (carry) our sins’? We do NOT find Scripture which supports the idea that the guilt of my sin was transferred to Christ. Christ offered Himself to be the sacrifice for sin (Heb 10:10-12), the propitiation for our sins (1Jo 2:1), to put away sin, even to be the forgiveness of sin. This great work of dealing with sin was accomplished without Him ever losing His condition as the Lamb without blemish.

There is one passage we should note on this topic, For he [God] hath made him [Jesus] to be sin for us, who [Jesus] knew no sin… –2Co 5:21. When we look at the Greek word in this verse translated as “sin” and compare this passage with all the other Scriptures, it seems the intended meaning for this phrase to be sin is more clearly defined as to be a sin offering. Christ’s soul was not blackened with the guilt of our sin, else He could not have retained His position … as of a lamb without blemish and without spot –1Pe 1:19. A proper understanding of the sense in which He took our sins is that He assumed the settlement for them.

c. “He took the wrath of God upon Himself.”

Concerning God’s wrath, we know that …he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him –Joh 3:36; …the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness –Rom 1:18; …and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others –Eph 2:3.

However, atonement was made, and then, in Romans, Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him –Rom 5:9. So, it is clear that the wrath of God toward us on account of sin is now averted when we are justified by His blood. However, the Scriptures do not say that Christ suffered the wrath of God. It may seem like a logical conclusion that if wrath was averted, and atonement was being made, then God›s wrath for sin must have fallen upon Christ, but that is not so stated in the scriptures. If we look at the picture of Abraham offering up his son Isaac, there was no wrath on Abraham’s part. Finally, God was “in Christ, reconciling the world unto Himself” and here what is emphasized is that Christ’s sacrifice to put away sin demonstrates to us the great love that the Father has toward us.

d. “God no longer looks at me; all He sees is Christ.”

The atonement should not be viewed, as perhaps many do, as a cloak for sin (to cover it). It is also sometimes stated this way: “Since Christ died on the cross for my sin, and I believe in Him, now Christ’s righteousness is all that God sees. When God looks at me, He no longer sees my sin; all He sees is Christ’s righteousness.” There is a great deal of error in this view, and the fruit of it is that many become complacent and tolerant of sin in their own lives. Through the atonement in Christ, God has made available to us everything needed for cleansing and to be made holy, but no, God does not credit Christ’s righteousness to our account. God’s purpose in the atonement was to make us righteous by purging our sin. We are to reckon ourselves dead unto sin, alive unto God. This does not mean that we have attained to a state of perfection, but we allow the atonement to be continually effective in our life.

For now, in section III, we are making summary statements, and in sections IV and V we are simply putting subheadings in place. Lord willing, we can take more time to flesh each one out in a future article. Until then, we encourage each one to do your own Bible study to more fully understand the whole of Scriptures’ teaching on the subject. Finally, it is our sincere desire that each of us would take heed that we are not deceived by the many voices from without and from within that Satan wishes to use to turn the church of Jesus Christ away from …the faith which was once delivered unto the saints. –Jud 1:3

III. What the Atonement does NOT do

a. Does NOT transfer guilt from one to another

As we stated above, our guilt did not blacken the soul of Christ. He provided atonement that our sins might be forgiven. He made, or was made, an offering for sin, and He was wounded for our transgressions, and by this act our sin is purged, and our guilt is taken away, without Him becoming guilty in our place.

b. Does NOT transfer righteousness from one to another—from Christ to us

Through Jesus our Lord we receive, given unto us, all things that pertain to life and godliness. We can say that our righteousness is only in Him, but we don’t say that His righteousness is somehow credited to our account when we are deficient. See also below on the issue of walking in the Light.

c. Does NOT protect us from harm/Does not build a hedge of protection around us

Our Sovereign Father provides our protection according to His will. Our protection does not come from the atonement, rather it comes out of our relationship with God as we walk by faith in obedience and draw near to Him. God protects, according to His will, those who are His. There is no guarantee that bad things will not happen, rather God promises that He will be with His children through whatever He allows them to go through.

d. Does not keep Satan away from us

Our Father does that according to His will (see Job 1 and 2, also 1 Cor 10:13). We do not need to “plead the blood for our protection” as though the blood of Christ was a means to ward off evil powers. We have the armor of God, shield of faith, and the sword of the Spirit, with all prayer, to overcome the powers of darkness.

IV. What the Atonement DOES do

  1. It reconciles
  2. It prepares a sacrifice for sin
  3. It provides a sin offering
  4. It redeems
  5. It ransoms
  6. It provides forgiveness of sins
  7. It provides remission of sins
  8. It cleanses us
  9. It enables God to see us as blameless
  10. It makes us righteous in God’s sight
  11. It causes believers to become a part of God’s family
  12. It causes believers to become brothers and sisters

V. What ALL was finished

  1. His suffering
  2. His temptations
  3. His labors on earth—His preaching and teaching
  4. The sacrificial system—sacrifices, which can never take away sins –Heb 10:11
  5. The law—was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ… –Gal 3:24
  6. Limited access to God—And the veil of the temple was rent in twain… –Mar 15:38

Quand Jésus eut donc reçu le vinaigre, il dit : C’est achevé : puis il inclina la tête et rendit l’esprit. –Jn 19:30

Au cours de l’année écoulée, tandis que nous élaborions cet article, nous avons pris de plus en plus conscience de l’intérêt croissant suscité par ce sujet. Divers articles et brochures ont été écrits, ou sont en cours de rédaction, à ce propos. Certains écrits débattent de théories particulières de l’expiation, tandis que d’autres réfléchissent à différents termes ou à des versets bibliques. Quelles idées et affirmations concernant l’expiation se trouvent dans les enseignements clairs de l’Écriture, et lesquelles relèvent de malentendus ou d’interprétations erronées ?

I. L’expiation

Le terme « expiation » est généralement compris comme désignant tout ou une partie de ce qui s’est produit spirituellement (pour le croyant) lorsque Christ a traversé ses souffrances, sa mort et sa résurrection. On emploie parfois le terme expiation pour définir ce qui amène les hommes et les femmes à être « un avec Dieu ». Comment cet événement historique continue-t-il de nous affecter aujourd’hui, quelque 2 000 ans plus tard ?

Dans ces discussions, on a tendance à oublier que l’œuvre achevée de Christ comprend plusieurs aspects, chacun produisant un effet différent pour le croyant aujourd’hui. Ces différents aspects comprennent les souffrances de Christ, son sang, sa mort, son ensevelissement, sa résurrection et son ascension.

a. Ses souffrances

Ses souffrances couvrent l’angoisse physique, émotionnelle et mentale qu’il a endurée et qui a culminé avec sa mort sur la croix. Nous voyons ici que …il fallait que le Christ souffrît, et qu’il ressuscitât des morts le troisième jour… et que la repentance et le pardon des péchés fussent prêchés en son nom… –Lc 24:46-47. Le serviteur souffrant, tel qu’il est décrit dans l’ensemble du chapitre 53 d’Ésaïe, donne une image saisissante de cet aspect de l’expiation. Ésaïe le décrit comme étant …blessé pour nos transgressions, [et] meurtri pour nos iniquités : –És 53:5. Nous trouvons aussi ici cette réalité : et c’est par ses meurtrissures que nous sommes guéris. –És 53:5. Enfin, nous voyons qu’il a été opprimé et affligé… –És 53:7, et qu’il a enduré …le travail de son âme… –És 53:11

Notons quelques autres passages, parmi les nombreux textes qui parlent de ses souffrances : Car Christ aussi a souffert une fois pour les péchés, lui juste pour des injustes, afin de nous amener à Dieu… –1 P 3:18 ; Bien qu’il fût Fils, il a appris l’obéissance par les choses qu’il a souffertes –Hé 5:8 ; Car il convenait que celui pour qui et par qui sont toutes choses, voulant conduire beaucoup de fils à la gloire, rendît parfait par les souffrances le chef de leur salut –Hé 2:10.

Un but parfois oublié des souffrances de Jésus est que, en tant que croyants, nous devons nous identifier à ses souffrances, comme le montrent les passages suivants : Car, de même que les souffrances de Christ abondent en nous, de même notre consolation abonde par Christ –2 Co 1:5 ; …si du moins nous souffrons avec lui, afin d’être aussi glorifiés avec lui –Rm 8:17 ; Afin de le connaître, lui, et la puissance de sa résurrection, et la communion de ses souffrances, en devenant conforme à sa mort –Ph 3:10.

b. Son sang versé

Le sang de Christ versé pour l’expiation de l’homme pécheur mérite un examen attentif en tant qu’aspect vital spécifique de l’ensemble. Bien sûr, il est inclus dans les points a. et c., mais les Écritures accordent également beaucoup d’attention à cette partie en particulier. Il faudrait peut-être tout un livre pour exposer cet aspect, mais retenons une chose à ce sujet. C’est par le sang versé de Jésus que nous recevons la solution précise de Dieu pour le pardon de nos péchés, exprimée ici par Jésus lui-même : Car ceci est mon sang, le sang de la nouvelle alliance, qui est répandu pour beaucoup, pour le pardon des péchés –Mt 26:28.

Dans les chapitres 9 et 10 de l’épître aux Hébreux, nous trouvons une explication très détaillée montrant que les « sacrifices de sang » de l’Ancien Testament n’étaient pas parfaits en eux-mêmes, mais constituaient un « type » annonçant le sacrifice parfait : Jésus, l’Agneau de Dieu. C’est dans ce contexte que nous lisons que …presque tout, selon la loi, est purifié avec du sang ; et sans effusion de sang, il n’y a pas de pardon. –Hé 9:22. Il est particulièrement important de s’en souvenir lorsque nous considérons que certains prétendent que Dieu aurait pu simplement pardonner le péché sans mort ni effusion de sang, s’il l’avait voulu. Ces personnes invoquent comme preuve le récit de Matthieu 18:23-35. Nous ferions bien de considérer que ce récit révèle le « pourquoi » (la compassion) du résultat, et non le « comment » des détails. Nous ne pouvons pas sortir ce récit du contexte des Écritures et bâtir une doctrine qui sape tout le reste des Écritures. Nous concluons donc que, dans l’ordre établi par Dieu, le péché doit être lavé par le sang de Christ —et de la part de Jésus-Christ, qui … nous a lavés de nos péchés dans son propre sang, –Ap 1:5.

Car tous ont péché et sont privés de la gloire de Dieu ; étant justifiés gratuitement par sa grâce, par la rédemption qui est en Jésus-Christ, que Dieu a établi comme propitiation, par la foi en son sang, afin de manifester sa justice pour le pardon des péchés commis auparavant, dans la patience de Dieu –Rm 3:23-25. Nous voyons ici que chacun de nous qui a péché (c’est-à-dire nous tous) bénéficie d’une propitiation rendue possible par la foi en son sang (celui de Jésus).

c. Sa mort

Jésus a dit : …je donne ma vie pour les brebis –Jn 10:15, et il a dit encore : …je donne ma vie, afin de la reprendre. Personne ne me l’ôte, mais je la donne de moi-même. J’ai le pouvoir de la donner et j’ai le pouvoir de la reprendre… –Jn 10:17-18.

Mais nous voyons Jésus, qui a été abaissé un peu au-dessous des anges à cause de la souffrance de la mort, couronné de gloire et d’honneur ; afin que, par la grâce de Dieu, il goûtât la mort pour tout homme. Car il convenait que celui pour qui et par qui sont toutes choses, voulant conduire beaucoup de fils à la gloire, rendît parfait par les souffrances le chef de leur salut. –Hé 2:9-10. Lorsque vous prenez la communion, …vous annoncez la mort du Seigneur, jusqu’à ce qu’il vienne –1 Co 11:26.

Ne savez-vous pas que nous tous qui avons été baptisés en Jésus-Christ, nous avons été baptisés en sa mort ? Nous avons donc été ensevelis avec lui par le baptême en sa mort, afin que, comme Christ est ressuscité des morts par la gloire du Père, nous aussi nous marchions en nouveauté de vie. –Rm 6:3-4

C’est durant cette période de la vie terrestre de Jésus que la partie terrestre et mortelle de sa personne s’est séparée de ce qui était céleste, éternel et immortel.

d. Son ensevelissement

Nous rappelons encore, comme indiqué ci-dessus, cette vérité : Nous avons donc été ensevelis avec lui par le baptême en sa mort… –Rm 6:4. Bien que tous ces aspects fassent partie de l’ensemble, l’ensevelissement représente …un grain de blé qui tombe en terre et meurt… –Jn 12:24. D’abord la vie prend fin (le sang est versé), puis vient la mort, ensuite l’ensevelissement, puis la résurrection. L’ensevelissement confirme que la mort a eu lieu. Il marque l’achèvement, la clôture et la fin de ce qui précédait. C’est l’intervalle nécessaire entre la mort et la résurrection.

C’est également le moment où Jésus est entré dans l’Hadès, le lieu des âmes défuntes, dont plusieurs passages des Écritures ne nous donnent que quelques aperçus.

e. Sa résurrection

Par sa résurrection, nous sommes ressuscités avec lui dans une vie nouvelle. (Romains 6:4) …en elle aussi vous êtes ressuscités avec lui, par la foi en l’action de Dieu, qui l’a ressuscité des morts –Col 2:12. Ainsi, par sa résurrection, nous sommes relevés avec lui d’entre les morts (si nous étions auparavant morts) et recevons la puissance de marcher en nouveauté de vie (la puissance de vaincre le péché).

f. Son ascension

Au sujet de son ascension, nous comprenons que …il fut élevé ; et une nuée le reçut et le déroba à leurs yeux. –Ac 1:9. C’est parce qu’il a quitté cette terre que nous bénéficions aujourd’hui de nombreux aspects essentiels de la vie du croyant. Le don du Saint-Esprit a été rendu possible après que Jésus eut quitté cette terre. Nous avons la promesse qu’il est allé nous préparer une meilleure demeure, afin que nous puissions le rejoindre un jour dans une joie éternelle. Jésus siège à la droite du trône de Dieu et intercède pour nous. Jésus remplit le rôle de notre souverain sacrificateur compatissant, qui connaît et comprend chacun de nos besoins et de nos combats, puisqu’il a fait l’expérience de vivre sur cette terre pécheresse dans un corps mortel.

Nous commençons ainsi à voir comment chaque partie de l’expiation produit un résultat différent pour le croyant, et que chaque partie n’est que cela : UNE PARTIE. Une partie de l’ensemble. Une partie de l’œuvre achevée de Christ. Chacune de ces listes pourrait se poursuivre sur des pages entières pour énumérer toutes les bénédictions et tous les bienfaits qu’elle rend possibles pour le croyant. Par souci de concision, nous allons nous arrêter là pour le moment et poursuivre le reste de l’article, mais nous espérons que cela incitera chacun de nous à méditer davantage ces sujets dans la Parole de Dieu.

II. Affirmations courantes qui ne sont pas conformes à la Bible

On entend parfois des affirmations populaires au sujet de l’expiation qui ne décrivent pas fidèlement ce que les Écritures enseignent. Mais parce qu’elles sont courantes dans nos conversations, ou qu’elles sont peut-être même les paroles d’un chant bien connu, elles peuvent fausser notre compréhension de l’œuvre achevée de Christ. À titre d’exemples, examinons les affirmations suivantes :

a. « Christ a pris ma place au Calvaire. »

Cela peut sembler une conclusion logique, puisqu’il est mort pour nous, …lui juste pour des injustes… –1 P 3:18. et qu’il est mort afin que nous vivions. Il ne fait aucun doute que c’était pour nous, mais la préposition « pour » peut s’entendre de plusieurs façons. Elle peut signifier à ma place ou en ma faveur. La plupart des passages des Écritures soulignent clairement qu’il est mort en ma faveur, mais l’idée d’une substitution directe est moins explicite. Insister sur la substitution nous conduit à l’idée suivante : il est mort à ma place, donc je n’ai pas à mourir. Si cette idée devient notre manière principale de concevoir l’expiation, nous risquons de passer à côté d’un point tout aussi important : puisqu’il est mort, je dois moi aussi mourir avec lui. Voir Rm 6:1-11

b. « La culpabilité de mon péché a été imputée à Christ. »

Certains passages disent que Christ a porté nos péchés. Ainsi Christ a été offert une seule fois pour porter les péchés de beaucoup… –Hé 9:28 et lui qui a porté lui-même nos péchés en son corps sur le bois… –1 P 2:24. Mais que signifie précisément « porter nos péchés » ? Nous ne trouvons PAS dans les Écritures de texte qui appuie l’idée que la culpabilité de mon péché a été transférée à Christ. Christ s’est offert en sacrifice pour le péché (Hé 10:10-12), en propitiation pour nos péchés (1 Jn 2:1), afin d’ôter le péché, et même d’être le pardon du péché. Cette grande œuvre accomplie pour traiter le péché a été réalisée sans qu’il perde jamais sa condition d’Agneau sans défaut.

Un passage mérite d’être relevé à ce sujet : Celui [Dieu] qui n’a point connu le péché, il [Jésus] l’a fait devenir péché pour nous… –2 Co 5:21. Lorsque nous examinons le mot grec traduit ici par « péché » et que nous comparons ce passage à tous les autres textes des Écritures, il semble que le sens voulu par l’expression devenir péché soit plus clairement défini comme devenir un sacrifice pour le péché. L’âme de Christ n’a pas été souillée par la culpabilité de notre péché, sinon il n’aurait pu conserver sa position …d’un agneau sans défaut et sans tache –1 P 1:19. Il faut comprendre correctement le sens dans lequel il a pris nos péchés : il en a assumé le règlement.

c. « Il a pris sur lui la colère de Dieu. »

Au sujet de la colère de Dieu, nous savons que …celui qui ne croit pas au Fils ne verra point la vie, mais la colère de Dieu demeure sur lui –Jn 3:36 ; …la colère de Dieu se révèle du ciel contre toute impiété et toute injustice des hommes qui retiennent injustement la vérité –Rm 1:18 ; …et nous étions par nature des enfants de colère, comme les autres –Ép 2:3.

Cependant, l’expiation a été accomplie, puis nous lisons dans l’épître aux Romains : À plus forte raison donc, maintenant que nous sommes justifiés par son sang, serons-nous sauvés par lui de la colère –Rm 5:9. Il est donc clair que la colère de Dieu contre nous à cause du péché est maintenant détournée lorsque nous sommes justifiés par son sang. Cependant, les Écritures ne disent pas que Christ a subi la colère de Dieu. On pourrait conclure logiquement que si la colère a été détournée et que l’expiation était accomplie, alors la colère de Dieu contre le péché a dû s’abattre sur Christ, mais cela n’est pas affirmé ainsi dans les Écritures. Si nous considérons le récit d’Abraham offrant son fils Isaac, Abraham n’éprouvait aucune colère. Enfin, Dieu était « en Christ, réconciliant le monde avec lui-même », et ce qui est souligné ici, c’est que le sacrifice de Christ pour ôter le péché nous démontre le grand amour que le Père a pour nous.

d. « Dieu ne me regarde plus ; il ne voit que Christ. »

Il ne faut pas considérer l’expiation, comme beaucoup le font peut-être, comme un voile qui couvrirait le péché. On l’exprime aussi parfois ainsi : « Puisque Christ est mort sur la croix pour mon péché et que je crois en lui, Dieu ne voit désormais que la justice de Christ. Quand Dieu me regarde, il ne voit plus mon péché ; il ne voit que la justice de Christ. » Cette conception comporte de nombreuses erreurs, et elle conduit beaucoup de personnes à devenir complaisantes et tolérantes envers le péché dans leur propre vie. Par l’expiation en Christ, Dieu a mis à notre disposition tout ce qui est nécessaire pour être purifiés et rendus saints ; mais non, Dieu ne porte pas la justice de Christ à notre compte. Le dessein de Dieu dans l’expiation était de nous rendre justes en purgeant notre péché. Nous devons nous considérer comme morts au péché et vivants pour Dieu. Cela ne signifie pas que nous ayons atteint un état de perfection, mais nous laissons l’expiation continuer d’agir dans notre vie.

Pour l’instant, dans la section III, nous présentons des affirmations récapitulatives, et dans les sections IV et V, nous nous contentons de mettre en place les sous-titres. Si le Seigneur le veut, nous pourrons développer chacun d’eux plus en détail dans un prochain article. D’ici là, nous encourageons chacun à étudier lui-même la Bible afin de mieux comprendre l’ensemble de l’enseignement des Écritures sur ce sujet. Enfin, nous souhaitons sincèrement que chacun de nous veille à ne pas se laisser tromper par les nombreuses voix, extérieures et intérieures, dont Satan veut se servir pour détourner l’Église de Jésus-Christ de …la foi qui a été transmise une fois pour toutes aux saints. –Jude 1:3

III. Ce que l’expiation ne fait PAS

a. Elle ne transfère PAS la culpabilité d’une personne à une autre

Comme nous l’avons dit plus haut, notre culpabilité n’a pas souillé l’âme de Christ. Il a accompli l’expiation afin que nos péchés puissent être pardonnés. Il a offert, ou a été fait, un sacrifice pour le péché ; il a été blessé pour nos transgressions, et par cet acte notre péché est purgé et notre culpabilité ôtée, sans qu’il devienne coupable à notre place.

b. Elle ne transfère PAS la justice d’une personne à une autre, de Christ à nous

Par Jésus notre Seigneur, nous recevons tout ce qui concerne la vie et la piété. Nous pouvons dire que notre justice se trouve uniquement en lui, mais nous ne disons pas que sa justice est en quelque sorte portée à notre compte lorsque nous sommes déficients. Voir aussi ci-dessous, au sujet de la marche dans la lumière.

c. Elle ne nous protège PAS du mal et ne forme pas une haie de protection autour de nous

Notre Père souverain nous protège selon sa volonté. Notre protection ne vient pas de l’expiation ; elle découle plutôt de notre relation avec Dieu, lorsque nous marchons par la foi dans l’obéissance et nous approchons de lui. Dieu protège ceux qui lui appartiennent, selon sa volonté. Rien ne garantit que de mauvaises choses ne se produiront pas ; Dieu promet plutôt qu’il sera avec ses enfants dans tout ce qu’il permet qu’ils traversent.

d. Elle ne tient pas Satan éloigné de nous

Notre Père agit ainsi selon sa volonté (voir Job 1 et 2, ainsi que 1 Co 10:13). Nous n’avons pas besoin de « plaider le sang pour notre protection », comme si le sang de Christ était un moyen de repousser les puissances du mal. Nous avons l’armure de Dieu, le bouclier de la foi et l’épée de l’Esprit, ainsi que toute prière, pour vaincre les puissances des ténèbres.

IV. Ce que l’expiation fait

  1. Elle réconcilie
  2. Elle prépare un sacrifice pour le péché
  3. Elle fournit un sacrifice pour le péché
  4. Elle rachète
  5. Elle paie une rançon
  6. Elle procure le pardon des péchés
  7. Elle procure la rémission des péchés
  8. Elle nous purifie
  9. Elle permet à Dieu de nous considérer comme irréprochables
  10. Elle nous rend justes aux yeux de Dieu
  11. Elle fait entrer les croyants dans la famille de Dieu
  12. Elle fait des croyants des frères et des sœurs

V. Tout ce qui a été achevé

  1. Ses souffrances
  2. Ses tentations
  3. Ses travaux sur terre : sa prédication et son enseignement
  4. Le système sacrificiel — des sacrifices qui ne peuvent jamais ôter les péchés –Hé 10:11
  5. La loi — était notre pédagogue pour nous conduire à Christ… –Ga 3:24
  6. L’accès limité à Dieu — Et le voile du temple se déchira en deux… –Mc 15:38

I have been told by many women folk here in Holmes County, Ohio, that we have excellent charity stores and second-hand shops, as is often the case where large groups of plain people are living. We have had people from all around come to visit, taking extra time to drop by these stores. Apparently, people here like to keep things in top shape, so at the first sign of wear, it’s “out with the old and in with the new.”

Likewise, no farmer would disagree that seeing all their machinery run like a top, and all their livestock stay healthy, is a satisfying feeling. Since the time of Adam, the Lord has always made us that way—to …have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth. –Gen 1:28

Having an opposite attitude is to be avoided. Jude exhorts us to beware of “certain men” who, within our midst, have “crept in unawares.” They live by the flesh and “despise dominion.” Two thousand years later, even in our overly casual society where “It’s all good” and we need to “Just chill,” the Lord still expects us to take seriously our calling to exercise God-given responsibility of dominion using Biblical principles in all that we do.

Does this dominion also extend to our own bodies? In Second Chronicles, Chapter 34, we can read of the wretched state of the Temple at the beginning of the reign of King Josiah, how he rebuilt it both physically with stone and timber—skillfully crafted by the artisans, and spiritually, by rediscovering and drinking in the Word of God. So too should we care for our bodies, as the Apostle Paul instructs us: What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God’s. –1Co 6:19-20

It is safe to say that judging by the multitude of nutritional supplements, chiropractors, doctors, and other various ancillary (supplemental) health care people and products, we make a good effort at keeping our physical temples well cared for and healthy. However, since we are all born with the curse of Adam, unlike machine parts that can simply be replaced, or a new machine purchased once the old one has run the full course of its life, we are faced with the reality that our body parts also have a practical “shelf life.” The older we get, the more apparent it is that life is very limited. The Bible says 70-80 years (–see Psa 90:10). (In America, in 2018, the average was 78.7 years. How little things have changed over 3 millennia later!)

I think we can all agree that God is primarily concerned about the spiritual temple, even more than the physical temple of our bodies. One doesn’t need to think hard to find godly men and women of today, and our spiritual forefathers of yesterday, who sacrificed and endured the destruction of their bodies, glorifying God, resulting in the cleansing of their souls and the future glorification of their bodies. Their plea was this: Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me. –Psa 51:10

Christ himself endured the destruction of His physical body, stating, …Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. –Joh 2:19. In the resurrection, his body was regenerated. We also read in scripture, about another physical regeneration, in which the earth will give birth to her dead; where those who dwell in the dust [will] wake up and shout for joy! (–see Isa 26:19)

Yet through this all, when our bodies break down or wear out, we feebly attempt, with some limited success, a physical regeneration of our own. There is a whole field of study focusing on Regenerative Medicine. The actual word “regeneration” literally means to “redo genesis” by recreating a new body—quite a lofty goal indeed!

Is there anything wrong with replacing broken parts (knees, hips and elbows), patching up broken pieces (bones and skin), and maintaining health in general (through good nutrition and physical activity)? Certainly not—it is how I make my living, advising and treating my patients! Yet like most things, even the pursuit of “good health” should give us pause to “count the costs” and exercise moderation—Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand. –Php 4:5. For while the pursuit of physical health is a good thing, it is a blind pursuit without regard to the spiritual costs (as we discovered in our series on vaccines), that can result in leading us astray and away from God.

There are two ditches on this road to physical health, spiritual health, and our overall well-being. In the ditch on the one hand, we can be reckless with our health, allowing our bodily temple to decay prematurely. Job said of man: Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass; –Job 14:5. So if we, through neglect, seek to cut those days short, are we not in defiance of God—seeking to short-circuit His perfect will for us? In the other ditch is the reckless and futile search for immortality—by seeking physical health at any cost. In doing so, is this not also an act of defiance? Paul reminds us: Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned: –Rom 5:12. In other words, due to sin, it is God’s plan for us to die physically (so that we may live eternally with Him).

Most readers, at this point would agree that both ends of the spectrum have this in common: they both neglect a person’s spiritual health, and they are both in a state of defiance toward God. So where am I going with this? Most Christians, who I know, do not pursue physical health at any cost. Bear with me then, as I would like to take the remainder of this article (and the next article) to give you a history of Regenerative Medicine—this “redoing of genesis.” Does it live up to its claims? Are there scams? What are the pitfalls? What does the future hold? Most importantly, how does it impact our spiritual health and our relationship with the Lord?

First, what exactly is Regenerative Medicine? As I mentioned previously, it literally means man’s efforts to “redo” genesis (origin, creation, or beginning). The term was first used as recently as the 1990s and is defined as the study and practice of “the replacement or regeneration of human cells, tissue, or organs, to restore or establish normal function.” In its short history, any and all means necessary to do this have been used.

It is different from Transplant Medicine in which whole organs are replaced but are still viewed as “foreign” by the receiving body. That is why strong anti-rejection medicines are needed for the rest of the individual’s life. It is also different from Orthopedic Medicine, in which hardware, such as screws, and titanium knees, for example, secure and replace warn out parts. Regenerative Medicine draws on the natural occurrence of certain organisms such as starfish, lizards, and lobsters, which are able to “regenerate” missing limbs and tails. In essence, the regenerated tissue is indistinguishable from the original, having few to no complications or side effects due to the fact that it is wholly integrated into that specific species’ host body. Sounds good doesn’t it?

This is not a new concept. Prometheus, in Greek mythology, was a “minor god,” who was punished by the “head god” Zeus (for “giving” fire to man) by having animals feast on his body, only to have his body regenerate the next day. A couple of thousand years later, Mary Shelly’s Frankenstein novel was subtitled “The Modern Prometheus.” This book, written almost exactly 200 years ago, contains a strong warning about unrestrained science, and man’s reckless search for fleshly regeneration. Even so, it is easy to see that man has had a long history of desire to regenerate his body, just as a mechanic swaps out parts or a starfish grows a new arm.

Advances in anesthesia, pharmacology (antibiotics and anti-rejection medicines in particular), surgery and sterilization techniques led to milestones in medicine, such as the first kidney transplant in 1954 and the first bone marrow transplant in 1968. But transplants had limitations—some injured and damaged tissues or complex organs, such as a brain, could not simply be replaced. Furthermore, due to an aging population and the sheer demands for the large quantities needed of some tissues, such as skin for burn victims, coupled with a chronic shortage of proper donors, alternatives were needed. Also, the dark shadow of tissue rejection was ever present and needed to be dealt with.

It has long been known that while an unborn child is a unique human being, it is rare for such developing children to be rejected by his or her mother’s body. We have learned this is due to the fact that in developing fetuses, their cells do not have many unique identifiers. The older a person becomes, the more their cells have a unique look and identification—kind of like the same fingerprint on the surface of each and every cell in a person’s body. A person’s body “knows” what its own tissue’s “fingerprint” looks like, and it “knows” that what isn’t native is foreign and must be attacked. By using fetal tissue, there would be almost no chance of rejection, and no need for dangerous life-long anti-rejection medicine. The new tissue would be entirely assimilated—so it was thought. So, attempts were made at using fetal tissue to cure things like Addison’s Disease (adrenal tissue) in the 1920s and Diabetes (pancreatic tissue) starting in the 1930s. While up to 24 fetuses were used per transplant, they eventually proved to be unsuccessful.1

By the 1990s, there was a renewed interest in using fetal tissue. Wouldn’t it be wonderful, some scientists thought, if, by simply inserting some fetal pancreatic insulin-producing cells under one’s forearms, diabetes could be cured? The same goes for fetal thyroid transplants, adrenal transplants—simply an outpatient procedure, and done in a few minutes. What about things like brain tissue for Parkinson’s disease or Alzheimer’s? The potential was seemingly limitless.

If that sounds somewhat macabre, there was an even more ominous side. It was shown experimentally in mice that one could successfully transplant fetal ovarian tissue.2 The idea was to transplant fetal ovarian tissue into infertile women (for example, survivors of childhood cancer in which the chemo rendered the girl infertile). This would sideline any “need” for IVF treatments. Imagine being a child born of a genetic mother that was aborted!

With the cultural abortion battles, there was an intense push to find a “cure.” Suppose there was a cure for Alzheimer’s or Diabetes? How many people would reject that cure if it came from fetal tissue? If they actually refused the treatment, how many of those people would voice their objection to abortion if a family member chose a curative (though unethical) treatment? If a parent of a diabetic child refused treatment, would it be considered child neglect, and would the state have grounds for forcibly treating the child or removing him or her from the home until treatment was received? In the end, one goal was that abortion would be justified in the minds of the population.

But something happened: The treatments didn’t work as planned in a significant number of patients. The treatments in a large number of Parkinson patients were actually described by the providing doctors as “catastrophic,” “absolutely devastating,” and “a real nightmare”.3 Instead of the classic muscle rigidity associated with Parkinson’s Disease, came jerking heads, flinging arms, and writhing bodies. The tissue did not “know” enough when to turn itself off, overproducing neurohormones, even forming tumors of skin, hair, and cartilage.4 Moreover, the tissue that “took” eventually died out by the same process that caused the Parkinson’s disease.5 The treatments were obviously stopped.

But at about this time, in the late 1990s, techniques were discovered that enabled researchers to isolate, and grow in great numbers, a certain cell called a “stem cell” from human embryos. Think of these rapidly growing stem cells as forming the stem of a plant. It is through them that the other types of cells are derived (leaves, flower, and fruit). These embryos, uniquely human, were obtained from “leftover” fertility treatments in which conception was initiated in a laboratory petri (glass) dish and allowed to grow to a cluster size. The desired cells were taken, and the rest destroyed. (In essence, these were “micro” abortions.)

Fetal tissue did not work as expected, partly because it was already too specialized and too “pre-programmed,” but also too impure, too costly, and too labor intensive—necessitating the harvesting of tissue from numerous aborted babies with a microscope and tweezers. Some scientists thought, why not obtain these stem cells, “program” them into the desired type of cell, and grow them to however many are needed?

In the next issue, I will tell you where the research currently stands, where there have been successes and failures, and how Christians can ethically navigate the turbulent waters of these times. It is amazing how the Lord opens doors, using the wonders of science, to create ethical alternatives for those who remain faithful to Him and His ways. It will be exciting to explain to you, how these “alternatives” have become the main focus of research and treatment for believers and unbelievers alike.

But before I leave you, I’d like to mention that over the years, I’ve had a number of people remark that these babies are being aborted anyway, so why not get some benefit from the tragedy, wouldn’t that be redemptive in a way?

Here is my (short list) of reasons why it would be unbiblical for Christians to benefit from unethical vaccines—and now fetal tissue treatments:

  1. The act of redemption cannot be separated from restitution and reconciliation. The very act of using fetal tissue only encourages further and expanded exploitation—just the opposite of restitution and reconciliation (where there needs to be a resolution to no longer repeat the sin). History has borne out that there is a multiplication of the sin, not the reduction. Where there was once one cell line, there are now dozens. Scientists are emboldened to do further, and even more unethical research, especially if there is no objection.

  2. The very word “redeem” means to purchase back something which was originally was yours, but now has become lost. The body of the unborn child was never ours to begin with, never ours to give, and never ours to profit from.

  3. Redemption always involves a sacrifice—of self. How can anyone sacrifice self by volunteering the body of another? (Heb 9:12) John 15:13 says, Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends. Some Christians are keen to use this verse to justify going to war. While there is definitely self-sacrifice in going to war, the goal is to make the enemy lay down THEIR lives. The utilitarian use of fetal tissue follows the same line of thinking, except that there is NO self-sacrifice in exploiting the body of an aborted baby.

  4. While Jesus’s redemption of mankind turned something horrid and ugly into something that glorifies God, it was an act of sanctification through holiness and righteousness. Regarding this issue, I can’t think of an act further removed from sanctification, holiness and righteousness—only opportunism. –see Psa 111:9 and 1 Co 1:30

  5. We cannot hope for the deliverance of God from evil—by participating in and benefiting from evil. We are forgiven our trespasses, only by forgiving, not by co-conspiring, only by repaying good for evil. –see Mat 5 & 6

  6. God finds the shedding of innocent blood abhorrent (He hates it!). –see Pro 6:17. We can only please God and can only receive atonement by purging ourselves from any association with this guilt—not by participating in it. –see Deu 21:8, 9. Can anyone imagine utilizing products such as soap and lamp shades made from holocaust victims who would have “died anyway”?

  7. When Saul destroyed the Amalekites, he kept the best of the loot—ostensibly as an offering to God (at least he said so when he was challenged by Samuel). –see 1 Sam 15 Why did God utterly reject His anointed king over this? Could it be that he did not want His chosen to profit or benefit from evil—even in the destruction of that evil? Could it be that by bringing the bounty of the wicked into the midst of his chosen people, His people risked becoming desensitized to that very same wickedness, and so became corrupted themselves? Samuel simultaneously wept and grieved over Saul, crying out to the Lord. If it is not us, then who will weep for us and for a fallen generation?

  8. The same could be said concerning the judgement of Achan’s secreted treasure following the defeat at Ai. In summary, if there is any personal benefit to be had following a tragedy or a judgement of another, the best way to tell if it is legitimate, is if the details are not cloaked in secrecy. (For the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth;) Proving what is acceptable unto the Lord. And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them. –Eph 5:9-11

  9. There are alternatives—why lend justification to unethical practices? On the issue of pursuing alternative vaccines, it is a difficult process, but not impossible to do. Following Christ often times follows the more arduous path, rather than the path of least resistance. The example of our faithful forefathers bears this out.

Tilsynelatende liker folk her å holde ting i topp stand, så ved det første tegn på slitasje er det «ut med det gamle og inn med det nye».

På samme måte vil ingen bonde være uenig i at det føles godt å se alle maskinene fungere som de skal og alt husdyret holde seg friskt. Helt siden Adams tid har Herren skapt oss slik: «…og råde over fiskene i havet og fuglene under himmelen og over alt levende som rører seg på jorden.» – 1 Mos 1,28

Vi må unngå å ha den motsatte holdningen. Judas formaner oss til å vokte oss for «visse mennesker» som «har sneket seg inn» blant oss. De lever etter kjødet og «forakter myndighet». To tusen år senere, selv i vårt altfor uformelle samfunn, der «alt er greit» og vi trenger å «bare slappe av», forventer Herren fortsatt at vi tar kallet vårt på alvor: å utøve det ansvaret Gud har gitt oss til å råde, i samsvar med bibelske prinsipper, i alt vi gjør.

Gjelder dette herredømmet også våre egne kropper? I Andre Krønikebok, kapittel 34, kan vi lese om den elendige tilstanden tempelet var i da kong Josjia begynte å regjere, og hvordan han bygde det opp igjen både fysisk, med stein og tømmer som håndverkerne bearbeidet dyktig, og åndelig, ved å gjenoppdage og ta til seg Guds ord. Slik bør også vi ta vare på kroppene våre, slik apostelen Paulus formaner oss: «Vet dere ikke at kroppen deres er et tempel for Den hellige ånd, som bor i dere og som dere har fra Gud? Dere tilhører ikke dere selv; dere er kjøpt, og prisen er betalt. Bruk da kroppen til Guds ære!» – 1 Kor 6,19–20

Det er trygt å si at vi, bedømt etter mengden av kosttilskudd, kiropraktorer, leger og andre ulike støttepersoner og produkter innen helsevesenet, gjør en god innsats for å holde våre fysiske templer godt ivaretatt og friske. Men siden vi alle er født med Adams forbannelse, og kroppsdelene våre i motsetning til maskindeler ikke bare kan skiftes ut, eller en ny maskin kjøpes når den gamle har nådd slutten av levetiden, må vi innse at også kroppsdelene våre har en praktisk «holdbarhetstid». Jo eldre vi blir, desto tydeligere er det at livet er svært begrenset. Bibelen sier 70–80 år (se Sal 90,10). (I Amerika var gjennomsnittet 78,7 år i 2018. Så lite har endret seg på over tre årtusener!)

Jeg tror vi alle kan være enige om at Gud først og fremst er opptatt av det åndelige tempelet, enda mer enn kroppens fysiske tempel. Det skal ikke mye ettertanke til for å finne gudfryktige menn og kvinner i dag, og våre åndelige forfedre fra tidligere tider, som ofret seg og utholdt at kroppene deres ble ødelagt for å herliggjøre Gud, noe som førte til at sjelene deres ble renset og kroppene deres en dag skal herliggjøres. Deres bønn lød slik: «Skap i meg et rent hjerte, Gud, gi meg en ny og stødig ånd!» – Sal 51,10

Kristus selv utholdt at hans fysiske kropp ble ødelagt, og sa: «…Riv ned dette tempelet, og jeg skal reise det opp på tre dager.» – Joh 2,19. I oppstandelsen ble kroppen hans gjenopprettet. Vi leser også i Skriften om en annen fysisk gjenopprettelse, da jorden skal føde sine døde, og de som bor i støvet, skal våkne og rope av glede! (Se Jes 26,19)

Likevel forsøker vi, når kroppene våre svikter eller slites ut, svakt og med begrenset hell å gjenopprette dem fysisk på egen hånd. Det finnes et helt forskningsfelt som retter seg mot regenerativ medisin. Selve ordet «regenerering» betyr bokstavelig talt å «gjøre skapelsen om igjen» ved å gjenskape en ny kropp – et svært ambisiøst mål!

Er det noe galt i å erstatte ødelagte deler (knær, hofter og albuer), reparere skadde deler (bein og hud) og generelt ta vare på helsen (gjennom god ernæring og fysisk aktivitet)? Absolutt ikke – det er slik jeg tjener til livets opphold, ved å gi råd til og behandle pasientene mine! Men som med det meste bør også jakten på «god helse» få oss til å stanse opp, «regne på kostnadene» og vise måtehold – «La alle mennesker få merke at dere er vennlige. Herren er nær.» – Fil 4,5. For selv om det er godt å strebe etter fysisk helse, kan en blind jakt uten hensyn til de åndelige kostnadene (slik vi oppdaget i serien vår om vaksiner) føre oss på villspor og bort fra Gud.

På veien mot fysisk helse, åndelig helse og generell velvære finnes det to grøfter. I den ene grøften kan vi opptre hensynsløst overfor helsen vår og la kroppens tempel forfalle før tiden. Job sa om mennesket: «Hans dager er fastsatt, tallet på hans måneder kjenner du. Du har satt hans grenser, han kan ikke gå over dem.» – Job 14,5. Hvis vi da gjennom forsømmelse prøver å forkorte disse dagene, setter vi oss ikke imot Gud – prøver vi ikke å kortslutte hans fullkomne vilje for oss? I den andre grøften ligger den hensynsløse og nytteløse jakten på udødelighet – ved å søke fysisk helse for enhver pris. Er ikke dette også en form for trass? Paulus minner oss på: «Synden kom inn i verden på grunn av ett menneske, og med synden kom døden. Og slik rammet døden alle mennesker fordi alle syndet.» – Rom 5,12. Med andre ord er det, på grunn av synden, Guds plan at vi skal dø fysisk (slik at vi kan leve evig sammen med ham).

De fleste leserne vil på dette punktet være enige i at begge ytterpunktene har dette til felles: De forsømmer begge en persons åndelige helse, og begge innebærer trass mot Gud. Hvor vil jeg med dette? De fleste kristne jeg kjenner, søker ikke fysisk helse for enhver pris. Vær derfor tålmodige med meg mens jeg bruker resten av denne artikkelen (og den neste) til å fortelle om historien til regenerativ medisin – denne «skapelsen om igjen». Lever den opp til påstandene sine? Finnes det svindel? Hva er fallgruvene? Hva bringer framtiden? Viktigst av alt: Hvordan påvirker den vår åndelige helse og vårt forhold til Herren?

Først: Hva er egentlig regenerativ medisin? Som jeg nevnte tidligere, betyr det bokstavelig talt menneskets forsøk på å «gjøre» skapelsen «om igjen» (opprinnelse, skapelse eller begynnelse). Begrepet ble først brukt så sent som på 1990-tallet og defineres som studiet av og praksisen med «å erstatte eller regenerere menneskeceller, vev eller organer for å gjenopprette eller etablere normal funksjon». I løpet av denne korte historien har man tatt i bruk alle mulige midler for å oppnå dette.

Dette er forskjellig fra transplantasjonsmedisin, der hele organer erstattes, men fortsatt oppfattes som «fremmede» av kroppen som mottar dem. Derfor er det nødvendig med sterke avstøtningshemmende medisiner resten av personens liv. Det er også forskjellig fra ortopedisk medisin, der festeanordninger, som skruer og for eksempel kneledd av titan, brukes til å feste og erstatte utslitte deler. Regenerativ medisin bygger på den naturlige evnen enkelte organismer, som sjøstjerner, øgler og hummere, har til å «regenerere» tapte lemmer og haler. I hovedsak er det regenererte vevet umulig å skille fra det opprinnelige, med få eller ingen komplikasjoner eller bivirkninger, fordi det er fullt integrert i vertskroppen til den aktuelle arten. Høres ikke det bra ut?

Dette er ikke noe nytt. I gresk mytologi var Prometheus en «mindre gud» som «hovedguden» Zevs straffet (for å ha «gitt» menneskene ilden) ved å la dyr spise av kroppen hans, som så ble gjenopprettet neste dag. Et par tusen år senere fikk Mary Shelleys roman Frankenstein undertittelen «Den moderne Prometheus». Denne boken, som ble skrevet for nesten nøyaktig 200 år siden, inneholder en sterk advarsel mot vitenskap uten grenser og menneskets hensynsløse jakt på å gjenopprette kroppen. Det er likevel lett å se at mennesket lenge har ønsket å gjenskape kroppen sin, akkurat som en mekaniker skifter ut deler eller en sjøstjerne får en ny arm.

Fremskritt innen anestesi, farmakologi (særlig antibiotika og avstøtningshemmende medisiner), kirurgi og steriliseringsteknikker førte til medisinske milepæler, som den første nyretransplantasjonen i 1954 og den første beinmargstransplantasjonen i 1968. Men transplantasjoner hadde begrensninger – skadde og ødelagte vev eller komplekse organer, som hjernen, kunne ikke bare erstattes. Dessuten var det behov for alternativer på grunn av en aldrende befolkning og den store etterspørselen etter de enorme mengdene som trengs av enkelte typer vev, som hud til brannskadde, i tillegg til en kronisk mangel på egnede donorer. Den mørke skyggen av vevsavstøtning var dessuten alltid til stede og måtte håndteres.

Det har lenge vært kjent at selv om et ufødt barn er et unikt menneske, er det sjelden at morens kropp avstøter barn som er under utvikling. Vi har lært at dette skyldes at cellene til fostre i utvikling ikke har mange unike kjennetegn. Jo eldre en person blir, desto mer unikt utseende og identitet får cellene – omtrent som om hver eneste celle i kroppen har det samme fingeravtrykket på overflaten. Kroppen «vet» hvordan «fingeravtrykket» til dens eget vev ser ut, og den «vet» at det som ikke hører hjemme der, er fremmed og må angripes. Ved å bruke fostervev ville det nesten ikke være noen risiko for avstøtning, og det ville ikke være behov for farlige avstøtningshemmende medisiner livet ut. Det nye vevet ville bli fullstendig innlemmet – slik trodde man. Derfor forsøkte man å bruke fostervev til å behandle tilstander som Addisons sykdom (binyrevev) på 1920-tallet og diabetes (bukspyttkjertelvev) fra 1930-tallet. Selv om det ble brukt opptil 24 fostre per transplantasjon, viste forsøkene seg etter hvert å være mislykkede.1

På 1990-tallet ble interessen for å bruke fostervev fornyet. Ville det ikke være fantastisk, tenkte enkelte forskere, om diabetes kunne kureres ganske enkelt ved å føre noen insulinproduserende celler fra fosterets bukspyttkjertel inn under underarmshuden? Det samme gjaldt transplantasjoner av fostervev fra skjoldbruskkjertelen og binyrene – bare et poliklinisk inngrep som kunne utføres på noen få minutter. Hva med hjernevev mot Parkinsons sykdom eller Alzheimers sykdom? Mulighetene virket ubegrensede.

Hvis dette høres nokså makabert ut, fantes det en enda mer illevarslende side. Forsøk på mus viste at det var mulig å transplantere eggstokkvev fra fostre.2 Tanken var å transplantere fostervev fra eggstokker til infertile kvinner (for eksempel kvinner som hadde overlevd kreft i barndommen, der cellegiftbehandlingen hadde gjort jenta infertil). Dette ville sette enhver «nødvendighet» av IVF-behandlinger til side. Tenk deg å være et barn født av en genetisk mor som ble abortert!

I takt med de kulturelle abortkampene ble det lagt et intenst press på å finne en «kur». Tenk om det fantes en kur mot Alzheimers sykdom eller diabetes? Hvor mange ville avvise kuren hvis den kom fra fostervev? Hvis de faktisk nektet behandling, hvor mange av dem ville protestere mot abort dersom et familiemedlem valgte en behandling som kunne kurere sykdommen (men var uetisk)? Hvis en forelder til et barn med diabetes nektet behandling, ville det bli regnet som omsorgssvikt, og ville staten ha grunnlag for å behandle barnet med tvang eller fjerne det fra hjemmet til det fikk behandling? Til syvende og sist var ett av målene å rettferdiggjøre abort i befolkningens øyne.

Men noe skjedde: Behandlingene virket ikke som planlagt hos et betydelig antall pasienter. Behandlingene av mange pasienter med Parkinsons sykdom ble faktisk omtalt av legene som utførte dem, som «katastrofale», «fullstendig ødeleggende» og «et virkelig mareritt».3 I stedet for den klassiske muskelstivheten som forbindes med Parkinsons sykdom fikk pasientene rykkende hoder, armer som flakset, og kropper som vred seg. Vevet «visste» ikke når det skulle slå seg av, og produserte for mye nevrohormoner; det dannet til og med svulster av hud, hår og brusk.4 Dessuten døde vevet som «slo rot», etter hvert ut gjennom den samme prosessen som forårsaket Parkinsons sykdom.5 Behandlingene ble åpenbart stanset.

Men omtrent på denne tiden, mot slutten av 1990-tallet, oppdaget man teknikker som gjorde det mulig for forskere å isolere og dyrke store mengder av en bestemt celletype, kalt «stamceller», fra menneskelige embryoer. Tenk på disse raskt voksende stamcellene som stammen på en plante. Det er fra dem de andre celletypene (blader, blomster og frukt) utvikles. Disse embryoene, som var unikt menneskelige, kom fra «til overs»-embryoer etter fertilitetsbehandlinger, der befruktning ble satt i gang i en laboratorie-petriskål (glasskål) og embryoene fikk vokse til en liten celleklump. De ønskede cellene ble tatt ut, og resten ble ødelagt. (I bunn og grunn var dette «mikro»-aborter.)

Fostervev virket ikke som forventet, delvis fordi det allerede var for spesialisert og «forhåndsprogrammert», men også for urent, for kostbart og for arbeidskrevende – det var nødvendig å høste vev fra mange aborterte barn ved hjelp av mikroskop og pinsett. Noen forskere tenkte: Hvorfor ikke hente ut disse stamcellene, «programmere» dem til den ønskede celletypen og dyrke så mange som trengs?

I neste utgave skal jeg fortelle hvor forskningen står i dag, hvor det har vært suksesser og fiaskoer, og hvordan kristne kan finne en etisk vei gjennom denne tidens urolige farvann. Det er fantastisk hvordan Herren åpner dører og bruker vitenskapens underverk til å skape etiske alternativer for dem som forblir trofaste mot ham og hans veier. Det blir spennende å forklare hvordan disse «alternativene» har blitt hovedfokus for forskning og behandling blant både troende og ikke-troende.

Men før jeg avslutter, vil jeg nevne at flere personer opp gjennom årene har bemerket at disse babyene uansett blir abortert, så hvorfor ikke få noe ut av tragedien – ville ikke det på en måte være forløsende?

Her er min (korte) liste over grunner til at det ville være ubibelsk for kristne å dra nytte av uetiske vaksiner – og nå også fostervevsbehandlinger:

  1. Forløsning kan ikke skilles fra godtgjørelse og forsoning. Selve bruken av fostervev oppmuntrer bare til ytterligere og mer omfattende utnyttelse – det stikk motsatte av godtgjørelse og forsoning (som innebærer at man beslutter å ikke gjenta synden). Historien har vist at synden øker, ikke minker. Der det en gang fantes én cellelinje, finnes det nå dusinvis. Forskere blir dristigere og utfører enda mer uetisk forskning, særlig hvis ingen protesterer.

  3. Forløsning innebærer alltid et offer – av en selv. Hvordan kan noen ofre seg selv ved å stille en annens kropp til rådighet? (Hebr 9,12) Johannes 15,13 sier: «Ingen har større kjærlighet enn den som gir livet for vennene sine.» Noen kristne er ivrige etter å bruke dette verset for å rettferdiggjøre det å gå i krig. Det er utvilsomt selvoppofrelse å dra i krig, men målet er å få FIENDEN til å gi SITT liv. Den utilitaristiske bruken av fostervev følger samme tankegang, bortsett fra at det IKKE innebærer noe selvoppofrelse å utnytte kroppen til et abortert barn.

  5. Vi kan ikke håpe på at Gud skal fri oss fra det onde ved å ta del i og dra nytte av det onde. Vi får tilgivelse for våre overtredelser bare ved å tilgi, ikke ved å inngå sammensvergelse, og bare ved å gjengjelde ondt med godt. Se Matt 5 og 6

  6. Gud avskyr at uskyldig blod blir utøst (han hater det!). Se Ordsp 6,17. Vi kan bare behage Gud og bare få soning ved å rense oss for enhver forbindelse med denne skylden – ikke ved å ta del i den. Se 5 Mos 21,8–9. Kan noen forestille seg å bruke produkter som såpe og lampeskjermer laget av holocaustofre som «uansett ville ha dødd»?

  7. Da Saul tilintetgjorde amalekittene, beholdt han det beste av byttet – angivelig som et offer til Gud (i hvert fall sa han det da Samuel utfordret ham). Se 1 Sam 15. Hvorfor forkastet Gud sin salvede konge fullstendig på grunn av dette? Kan det være fordi han ikke ønsket at sine utvalgte skulle tjene på eller dra nytte av det onde – ikke engang når det onde ble tilintetgjort? Kan det være at når den ugudeliges bytte ble ført inn blant hans utvalgte folk, risikerte folket å bli ufølsomt overfor den samme ondskapen og dermed selv bli fordervet? Samuel gråt og sørget samtidig over Saul og ropte til Herren. Hvis det ikke er oss, hvem skal da gråte for oss og for en fallen generasjon?

  8. Det samme kan sies om dommen over Akans skjulte skatt etter nederlaget ved Ai. Kort sagt: Hvis det finnes en personlig fordel å hente etter en tragedie eller en dom over en annen, er den beste måten å avgjøre om den er legitim, å se om detaljene ikke er innhyllet i hemmelighold. «Åndens frukt er all godhet, rettferdighet og sannhet. Prøv hva som er til glede for Herren. Ha ikke noe med mørkets ufruktbare gjerninger å gjøre, men avslør dem.» – Ef 5,9–11

  9. Det finnes alternativer – hvorfor gi uetisk praksis legitimitet? Når det gjelder å søke etter alternative vaksiner, er det en vanskelig prosess, men ikke umulig. Å følge Kristus innebærer ofte å velge den mer krevende veien framfor den veien som yter minst motstand. Våre trofaste forfedres eksempel viser dette.
